items.new: The long and narrow peninsula of Malacca, extending southeast from the territories of Burma, forms the most southerly point of all Asia. In a continuous line from that peninsula stretch the long islands of Sumatra, Java, Bali, and Timor. These, with many others, form a vast mole, or rampart, lengthwise connecting Asia with New Holland and dividing the long unbroken Indian Ocean from the densely studded eastern archipelagoes. This rampart is pierced by several sally-ports for the convenience of ships and whales, the most prominent being the Straits of Sunda and Malacca. By the Straits of Sunda, chiefly, vessels bound to China from the west emerge into the China seas.

items.new: Those narrow Straits of Sunda divide Sumatra from Java. Standing midway in that vast rampart of islands, buttressed by that bold green promontory known to seamen as Java Head, they closely resemble the central gateway opening into some vast walled empire. And considering the inexhaustible wealth of spices, silks, jewels, gold, and ivory with which the thousand islands of that eastern sea are enriched, it seems a significant provision of nature that such treasures, by the very formation of the land, should at least bear the appearance — however ineffective — of being guarded from the all-grasping western world. The shores of the Straits of Sunda are unsupplied with those domineering fortresses which guard the entrances to the Mediterranean, the Baltic, and the Propontis (the Sea of Marmara). Unlike the Danes, these Orientals do not demand the obsequious homage of lowered topsails from the endless procession of ships running before the wind that for centuries past, by night and day, have passed between the islands of Sumatra and Java, freighted with the costliest cargoes of the east. But while they freely waive such ceremony, they by no means renounce their claim to more solid tribute.

items.new: But what now? In this globe-girdling quest, does Ahab touch no land? Does his crew drink air? Surely he will stop for water. No. For a long time now, the circus-running sun has raced within his fiery ring and needs no sustenance but what is in himself. So with Ahab. Notice this, too, about the whaler. While other ships are loaded down with foreign goods to be transferred to distant wharves, the world-wandering whale-ship carries no cargo but herself and her crew, their weapons and their wants. She has a whole lake's contents bottled in her ample hold. She is ballasted with useful things, not entirely with useless pig-lead and ballast iron. She carries years' worth of water in her. Clear old prime Nantucket water, which, when three years at sea, the Nantucketer in the Pacific prefers to drink over the brackish fluid rafted off only yesterday in casks from Peruvian or Indian streams. Hence it is that while other ships may have gone to China from New York and back again, touching at a score of ports, the whale-ship in all that time may not have sighted one grain of soil — her crew having seen no man but floating seamen like themselves. So that if you brought them the news that another flood had come, they would only answer: "Well, boys, here's the ark!"

But when the swift Pequod, with a fresh leading wind, was herself in hot chase — how very kind of these tawny philanthropists to help speed her on to her own chosen pursuit, serving as mere riding-crops and spurs to her. Some such thought seemed to be Ahab's as he paced the deck with glass under arm, in his forward turn beholding the monsters he chased and in his after turn the bloodthirsty pirates who were chasing him, the chaser. And when he glanced upon the green walls of the watery passage through which the ship was sailing, and considered that through that gate lay the route to his vengeance, and saw how through that same gate he was now both chasing and being chased to his deadly end — and not only that, but a herd of remorseless wild pirates and inhuman atheistical devils were infernally cheering him on with their curses — when all these thoughts had passed through his brain, Ahab's brow was left gaunt and furrowed, like a black sand beach after some stormy tide has been gnawing it without being able to drag the firm thing from its place.

items.new: Stripped to our shirts and drawers, we sprang to the oars. After several hours' pulling, we were almost ready to give up the chase when a general pausing commotion among the whales gave encouraging signs that they were now under the influence of that strange paralysis of indecision which, when fishermen see it in a whale, they say he is gallied. The compact martial columns in which they had been rapidly and steadily swimming now broke apart in one measureless rout. Like King Porus's elephants in the Indian battle with Alexander, they seemed going mad with panic. Expanding in vast irregular circles in all directions, swimming aimlessly this way and that, they plainly showed their distracted terror by their short, thick spoutings. This was still more strangely shown by those among them who, completely paralyzed as it were, helplessly floated like waterlogged dismasted ships on the sea. Had these leviathans been but a flock of simple sheep pursued over a pasture by three fierce wolves, they could not possibly have shown such excessive dismay. But this occasional timidity is characteristic of almost all herding creatures. Though banding together in tens of thousands, the lion-maned buffaloes of the West have fled before a solitary horseman. Witness, too, all human beings — how when herded together in the sheepfold of a theater pit, they will at the slightest alarm of fire rush helter-skelter for the exits, crowding, trampling, jamming, and mercilessly crushing each other to death. So it is best to withhold any amazement at the strangely gallied whales before us, for there is no folly of the beasts of the earth which is not infinitely outdone by the madness of men.

items.new: All whaleboats carry certain curious devices, originally invented by the Nantucket Indians, called druggs. Two thick squares of wood of equal size are stoutly clenched together so that they cross each other's grain at right angles. A line of considerable length is then attached to the middle of this block, and the other end of the line, being looped, can in a moment be fastened to a harpoon. It is chiefly among gallied whales that this drugg is used. For then, more whales are close around you than you can possibly chase at one time. But sperm whales are not encountered every day, so while you can, you must kill all you can. And if you cannot kill them all at once, you must wound them so that they can be killed afterward at your leisure. Hence it is that at times like these the drugg comes into play. Our boat was furnished with three of them. The first and second were successfully thrown, and we saw the whales staggering off, fettered by the enormous sideways resistance of the towing drugg. They were hobbled like criminals with ball and chain. But when we flung the third, the clumsy wooden block, as it was being tossed overboard, caught under one of the boat's seats and in an instant tore it out and carried it away, dumping the oarsman into the boat's bottom as the seat slid from under him. On both sides the sea poured in at the damaged planks, but we stuffed two or three pairs of drawers and shirts in, and so stopped the leaks for the time being.

At any rate — though such a measurement at such a time might be deceptive — spouts could be seen from our low boat that seemed to play up almost from the rim of the horizon. I mention this because these smaller whales, now and then visiting our becalmed boat from the margin of the lake, showed a wondrous fearlessness and confidence, or else a spellbound panic that was impossible not to marvel at — whether because the cows and calves had, as it were, been purposely locked up in this innermost fold, and the wide extent of the herd had prevented them from learning the precise cause of its stopping, or possibly because they were so young, unsophisticated, and in every way innocent and inexperienced; however it may have been. Like household dogs, they came snuffling right up to our gunwales and touching them, until it almost seemed that some enchantment had suddenly domesticated them. Queequeg patted their foreheads. Starbuck scratched their backs with his lance, though, fearful of the consequences, he refrained from darting it for the time.

items.new: When serenely traveling on one of these journeys, if any strange suspicious sights are seen, the lord whale keeps a wary eye on his interesting family. Should any rudely bold young Leviathan happen that way and presume to draw confidentially close to one of the ladies — with what prodigious fury the Bashaw (the pasha) assails him and chases him away! A fine state of affairs indeed, if unprincipled young rakes like him are to be permitted to invade the sanctity of domestic bliss. Though do what the Bashaw will, he cannot keep the most notorious Lothario out of his bed, for alas, all fish bed in common. As on shore, the ladies often cause the most terrible duels among their rival admirers. Just so with the whales, who sometimes come to deadly battle, and all for love. They fence with their long lower jaws, sometimes locking them together and striving for supremacy like elks that interlock their antlers in war. Not a few are captured bearing the deep scars of these encounters: furrowed heads, broken teeth, scalloped fins, and in some instances wrenched and dislocated mouths.

Gently he insinuates his vast bulk among them again and revels there awhile, still in tantalizing proximity to young Lothario, like pious Solomon devoutly worshipping among his thousand concubines. If other whales are in sight, the fishermen will seldom give chase to one of these Grand Turks, for these Grand Turks are too lavish with their strength, and hence their oil-yield is small. As for the sons and daughters they beget, those sons and daughters must take care of themselves — at least with only the mother's help. For like certain other omnivorous roving lovers that might be named, the lord whale has no taste for the nursery, however much for the bower. And so, being a great traveler, he leaves his anonymous babies all over the world, every baby an exotic. In good time, nevertheless, as the ardor of youth declines — as years and gloom increase, as reflection lends her solemn pauses — in short, as a general weariness overtakes the sated Turk, a love of ease and virtue replaces the love of maidens. Our Ottoman enters upon the impotent, repentant, lecturing stage of life, forswears and disbands the harem, and grown to an exemplary, sulky old soul, goes about all alone among the meridians and parallels saying his prayers and warning each young Leviathan from his amorous errors.

items.new: Some fifty years ago there was a curious case of whale-trover (a suit to recover the value of goods wrongfully taken) litigated in England. The plaintiffs stated that after a hard chase of a whale in the northern seas, and when they had succeeded in harpooning the fish, they were at last, through peril of their lives, obliged to abandon not only their lines but their boat itself. Eventually the defendants — the crew of another ship — came up with the whale, struck, killed, seized, and finally claimed it before the very eyes of the plaintiffs. And when those defendants were confronted, their captain snapped his fingers in the plaintiffs' faces and assured them that by way of a doxology (a closing hymn of praise) to the deed he had done, he would now retain their line, harpoons, and boat, which had remained attached to the whale at the time of the seizure. So the plaintiffs sued for the recovery of the value of their whale, line, harpoons, and boat.

items.new: Is it not a saying on everyone's lips that possession is half the law — regardless of how the thing came into possession? But often possession is the whole of the law. What are the bodies and souls of Russian serfs and Republican slaves but Fast-Fish, of which possession is the whole of the law? What to the greedy landlord is the widow's last mite but a Fast-Fish? What is yonder undetected villain's marble mansion with a door-plate for a waif — what is that but a Fast-Fish? What is the ruinous discount that Mordecai the broker gets from poor Woebegone the bankrupt, on a loan to keep Woebegone's family from starving — what is that ruinous discount but a Fast-Fish? What is the Archbishop of Savesoul's income of £100,000, seized from the meager bread and cheese of hundreds of thousands of broken-backed laborers, all sure of heaven without any of Savesoul's help — what is that globular £100,000 but a Fast-Fish? What are the Duke of Dunder's hereditary towns and hamlets but Fast-Fish? What to that mighty harpooner John Bull is poor Ireland but a Fast-Fish? What to that apostolic lancer Brother Jonathan (the United States) is Texas but a Fast-Fish? And concerning all these, is not Possession the whole of the law?

Now the Cinque Ports are partially or somehow under the jurisdiction of a sort of policeman or beadle (a minor parish officer) called a Lord Warden. He holds the office directly from the crown, I believe, and all the royal revenues from the Cinque Port territories become his by assignment. Some writers call this office a sinecure. But not so. Because the Lord Warden is busily employed at times in pocketing his perquisites — which are his chiefly by virtue of that same pocketing of them.

items.new: In outward appearance, Pip and Dough-Boy made a match, like a black pony and a white one, of equal size though different color, driven together as one eccentric team. But while hapless Dough-Boy was by nature dull and sluggish in his wits, Pip, though over tender-hearted, was at bottom very bright, with that pleasant, warm, jolly brightness peculiar to his tribe — a tribe who ever enjoy all holidays and festivities with finer, freer relish than any other race. For blacks, the year's calendar should show nothing but three hundred and sixty-five Fourth of Julys and New Year's Days. Nor smile while I write that this little black boy was brilliant, for even blackness has its brilliance: behold that lustrous ebony, paneled in kings' cabinets. But Pip loved life and all life's peaceful securities, so that the panic-striking business in which he had somehow become entangled had most sadly dimmed his brightness — though, as will soon be seen, what was thus temporarily subdued in him was destined in the end to be luridly illuminated by strange wild fires, that falsely showed him off to ten times the natural luster with which, in his native Tolland County in Connecticut, he had once enlivened many a fiddler's dance on the green and, at melodious twilight, with his gay ha-ha! had turned the round horizon into one star-belled tambourine. So, though in the clear light of day a pure diamond drop suspended against a blue-veined neck will glow with healthy beauty, yet when the cunning jeweler would show you the diamond in its most impressive luster, he lays it against a gloomy background and then lights it up not by the sun but by some unnatural gas. Then come those fiery blazes, infernally superb. Then the evil-blazing diamond, once the divinest symbol of the crystal skies, looks like some crown-jewel stolen from the King of Hell. But let us get to the story.

items.new: As soon as he recovered himself, the poor little negro was assailed by yells and curses from the crew. Calmly letting these irregular damnations blow over, Stubb then in a plain, businesslike, but still half-humorous manner, cursed Pip officially. And that done, unofficially gave him much wholesome advice. The substance was: Never jump from a boat, Pip, except — but all the rest was indefinite, as the soundest advice ever is. Now, in general, "Stick to the boat" is the true motto in whaling. But cases will sometimes arise when "Leap from the boat" is still better. Moreover, as if realizing at last that if he gave Pip fully conscientious advice, he would be leaving him too wide a margin to jump in for the future, Stubb suddenly dropped all counsel and concluded with a flat command: "Stick to the boat, Pip, or by the Lord, I won't pick you up if you jump. Mind that. We can't afford to lose whales because of the likes of you. A whale would sell for thirty times what you would, Pip, in Alabama. Bear that in mind, and don't jump anymore." By this, perhaps, Stubb indirectly hinted that though man loved his fellow, yet man is a money-making animal, a tendency that too often interferes with his kindness.

items.new: But we are all in the hands of the Gods, and Pip jumped again. It was under very similar circumstances to the first time, but now he did not carry the line overboard with him. And so when the whale started to run, Pip was left behind on the sea, like a hurried traveler's trunk. Alas! Stubb was but too true to his word. It was a beautiful, bountiful, blue day. The spangled sea was calm and cool, stretching flatly away on all sides to the horizon, like gold-beater's skin hammered out to the extreme. Bobbing up and down in that sea, Pip's ebony head showed like a head of cloves. No boat-knife was lifted when he fell so rapidly astern. Stubb's inexorable back was turned upon him, and the whale was winged. In three minutes, a whole mile of shoreless ocean lay between Pip and Stubb. Out from the center of the sea, poor Pip turned his crisp, curling, black head to the sun — itself another lonely castaway, though the loftiest and the brightest.
